title: Business Management SL and HL · Set B · Paper 1
subject: business-management

resources.title: Unseen case study · Sundial Sound
resources.text:
When Sundial Sound began, its founder also edited every recording. Its 11 employees now work with 26 freelance narrators. Small public libraries have relied on its unusual local-language catalogue for five years. Each library buys a one-year licence. This allows unlimited loans of a title to members of that library, but only one user may listen to the title at any given time. Libraries pay at the start of the licence period.

The company has two objectives for the next year. It wants to earn sufficient profit to finance accessible editions with descriptions of visual material. It also wants to increase access in areas where sales of printed books are low. Its accountant has warned that developing new titles before libraries sign contracts ties up cash. The founder’s younger brother, a director, would prefer to treat all new production as an opportunity for growth.

| Indicator | Two years ago | Last year |
|---|---:|---:|
| Annual library licence revenue / CU | 192,000 | 216,000 |
| Number of subscribing libraries | 80 | 96 |
| Eligible libraries that renewed | 90% | 82% |
| New titles recorded | 24 | 36 |

Several libraries joined on discounted trial licences during the last year. The head librarian at a long-standing customer said that some members wait six weeks for a popular title while other titles are seldom borrowed. Library managers receive annual usage reports. They cannot yet see current queues. Independently, a narrator proposed recording brief extracts for use in promotion. Narrators would have to consent to having their voices used in advertisements.

Luma, an established streaming platform, offers a two-year distribution agreement. It will pay a fixed CU 90,000 fee each year for exclusive access to Sundial’s twelve most popular titles on personal streaming services. Sundial can still sell those titles to libraries. Luma expects to attract new listeners through its own promotion, but it will determine the consumer price and will share only quarterly totals. Authors receive a royalty for each title used commercially. Sundial has yet to settle what Luma plays will count as a royalty-bearing use.

Sundial’s editor fears that the platform will favour the best-selling language and discourage investment in smaller audiences. A librarian argues that easier personal access could reduce queues and make libraries more willing to renew. Another librarian argues that members may instead expect the library to cancel licences for titles available elsewhere.

An alternative is a six-month library pilot. For a small supplement, a library could allow up to three users to listen to a popular title at once and see weekly waiting lists. Eight urban libraries volunteered after receiving an invitation by email. Staff would interview librarians and compare renewal intentions with actual renewals later. No rural library volunteered. Running the pilot would take two staff away from preparations for six forthcoming titles. The board must choose whether to sign Luma’s current terms, negotiate changes or give priority to the pilot.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage change in average annual licence revenue per subscribing library.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain one possible conflict between Sundial’s objectives.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to Sundial of the outsourcing arrangement with narrators.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Explain two limitations of using the eight volunteers to predict renewal by all libraries.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: Explain two ways weekly usage information could improve a library’s purchasing decisions.

steps.text: Income generated by the sale of goods or services.
It is measured before deducting costs, for example total licence fees earned.
A decrease of 6.25%.
Serving small-language audiences supports access.
Production costs are incurred before the licence sales are known.
Low demand could leave less profit to finance accessible editions.
Freelancers give access to language-specific voices as titles require them.
Sundial can acquire the skill without year-round salaries.
Freelancers control their schedules or voice-use permissions.
Releases or promotional extracts may be delayed while consent or availability is secured.
The sample excludes rural libraries.
Urban demand and queues may differ from rural use.
Volunteers selected themselves after an email invitation.
Those already interested in simultaneous access may express greater willingness to renew than other libraries.
Queue data can identify titles where one-user licences limit access.
Paying for extra simultaneous users could help more members at those sites.
Low-use titles can also be identified.
Shifting a limited budget to better-used titles can raise the value of a renewal.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether Sundial should accept Luma’s proposed agreement.

steps.text: Two years of CU 90,000 payments could fund new accessible editions and reduce revenue uncertainty. Exposure may draw listeners to lesser-known titles, but Luma controls pricing, selects the twelve strongest titles and shares little information. Clarify royalties and estimate the effect of lost renewals before treating the entire fee as incremental profit. Retaining library rights helps protect the core market. Negotiate reporting rights, a royalty definition and a trial or reject the current offer if the downside exceeds the fee. Use best fit. Award 0 for no creditable response, 1–2 for limited assertions, 3–4 for a partially explained point with weak application, 5–6 for developed analysis using case evidence, 7–8 for supported consideration of competing arguments and a reasoned decision, and 9–10 for sustained evaluation integrating specific evidence, a material limitation and a convincing judgement. Credit a well-supported alternative.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Discuss whether Sundial should give priority to the library pilot over producing the six forthcoming titles.

steps.text: Waiting lists and the fall in renewal from 90% to 82% suggest a retention problem. Multiple access and weekly queue information address an identified need. Volunteers are unrepresentative and renewal intentions may not become sales. Delaying six titles could disappoint smaller-language audiences. Extend the pilot to matched rural and urban libraries, track actual renewals and limit staff time. A staggered release is defensible where authors or libraries already expect the titles.
